what_it_does: Adenosine is used in skincare mainly as a skin-conditioning, anti-aging support ingredient.
summary_short: Adenosine is a naturally occurring nucleoside involved in cell signaling. The provided evidence is mostly medical and neurological, not cosmetic, so direct skincare conclusions are limited. No EU or US restriction is noted here.
summary_long:
Adenosine is a purine nucleoside that interacts with cell-surface adenosine receptors and helps regulate many physiological signals. The supplied abstracts describe roles in pain signaling, inflammation, seizures, and tumor biology, but they do not directly test topical cosmetic use on skin [PMID:unknown].

Mechanistically, adenosine can act through adenosine receptors such as A1 and A2 receptors. In one mouse acupuncture study, local adenosine release was linked to A1 receptor-mediated anti-nociceptive effects, suggesting adenosine can influence local sensory signaling under certain conditions [PMID:unknown]. Other reviews describe adenosine as a short-lived signaling molecule because it is rapidly taken up into nearby cells and metabolized.

The evidence quality for skincare-specific claims is thin in the provided sources. These abstracts support that adenosine is biologically active in the body, but they do not provide controlled human cosmetic data, wrinkle measurements, barrier outcomes, pigmentation effects, or topical skin penetration data.

No typical cosmetic concentration is mentioned in the supplied abstracts. Because the sources are not formulation studies, they also do not identify ideal pH, delivery systems, or whether adenosine works better in creams, serums, or gels.

The abstracts do not report topical irritation or cosmetic safety outcomes. They also do not mention common skincare pairings or conflicts, so no ingredient-combination claims can be made from this evidence alone.
